chapter.name: Universal Franchise and India's Electoral System

questions.q: At a panchayat meeting in a village near Nashik, a landowner with 50 acres argues that his vote should count for more than a farm labourer's, because he owns more of the village's land. Which principle of the chapter answers him directly?
questions.a: Every adult citizen gets one vote, and all votes have equal value
o: Every adult citizen gets one vote, and all votes have equal value
A voter must be registered as a voter in her own constituency first
No one can vote on another person's behalf in any election
A person guilty of certain serious crimes is barred from voting

questions.q: Rohan argues: 'Equal value means that every voter has one vote and no vote counts more because of caste, wealth or education. That is why every winning candidate must have received more than half of all the votes.' Test his two claims and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. His first sentence is right: every adult citizen gets one vote and all votes have equal value irrespective of caste, creed, race, religion, gender, education or income. His second does not follow: equal value says nothing about how many votes a winner gets. Under First-Past-the-Post the candidate with the most votes wins, even without 50 per cent, as Gurmat did in the class election with 12 votes against Ravi's 10 and Ahmed's 8.
s: Verdict: partly right
First claim is right: one vote each, equal value
Second claim is wrong: the most votes wins, even below half, with Gurmat's example

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Universal adult franchise does not mean that every adult citizen can cast a vote at any polling booth she chooses.
Reason (R): To exercise the right, a citizen must be registered as a voter in her own constituency.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? 'Universal adult franchise means that every citizen aged 18 and above votes directly in every election held in India, including the election of the President.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. Universal franchise covers the elections to the Lok Sabha, the legislative assembly of every state and union territory, and all local elections in villages and cities (Article 326). The President is not elected directly by the people but by an electoral college of elected MPs and MLAs.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: universal franchise covers Lok Sabha, assembly and local elections; the President is chosen by an electoral college of elected representatives

questions.q: India changed the minimum voting age from 21 to 18 in 1988. (a) How many one-year age groups gained the vote at once? (b) Give one argument for the change, based on a reason the chapter gives for why universal franchise matters. (c) Name one condition that the change did NOT remove for these new voters.
questions.a: (a) Three age groups: those aged 18, 19 and 20. (b) For example: 'everyone's voice matters' or 'power to determine one's future': young adults also live with the results of elections and get a say in the nation's future. (c) For example, they still had to be registered as voters in their own constituency (or be citizens) before they could vote.
s: Part (a): three age groups (18, 19, 20)
Part (b): an argument tied to a reason from the chapter's list
Part (c): one condition still needed, e.g. registration in one's own constituency

questions.q:
Read the statements about the right to vote in India.
1. A citizen who has turned 18 but is not registered as a voter in her constituency cannot yet exercise her right to vote.
2. Under universal adult franchise, the vote of a graduate carries more value than the vote of a person who never went to school.
3. A person found guilty of committing certain serious crimes is barred from voting.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
(a) What does the word 'universal' rule out in 'universal adult franchise'?
(b) Using your answer, explain why a rule that let only people who can read vote would break the principle, even if the age rule stayed at 18.
questions.a: (a) It rules out leaving anyone out on grounds of caste, creed, race, religion, gender, education, income and the like: every adult citizen gets one vote. (b) Reading ability depends on education, which is one of the grounds the principle rules out; such a rule would deny adult citizens a vote they are entitled to, whatever their age.
s: Part (a): no exclusion on caste, creed, race, religion, gender, education or income
Part (b): a literacy rule excludes on the basis of education, so it breaks universality

questions.q: A state is drafting four new rules for its municipal elections. Which rule would go AGAINST universal adult franchise as this chapter defines it?
questions.a: Only people who pay property tax may vote for councillors
o: Only people who pay property tax may vote for councillors
Every voter must be registered as a voter in her own constituency
A son may not vote in place of his absent mother
A person guilty of certain serious crimes is barred

questions.q:
A presiding officer at a booth in a village in Odisha writes four entries in her diary on polling day.
Entry 1: A girl of 17 asked to vote because her whole family was voting; she was sent home.
Entry 2: A man said his wife was at work and asked to vote in her place; a volunteer let him.
Entry 3: A man registered in Cuttack asked to vote here because he was visiting relatives; he was sent away.
Entry 4: A landowner asked for two ballot papers because he owns most of the village land; he was refused.
(a) Which entry records a breach of the rules, and which rule was broken?
(b) Which rule justified sending the Cuttack voter away?
(c) Which principle of universal franchise backs the refusal in Entry 4?
(d) The girl in Entry 1 will turn 18 in 14 months, and the next election at this booth is in 2 years. Predict whether she will be able to vote at that election, and name the one thing she must still do.
questions.a: (a) Entry 2: no one can vote on another's behalf, so the volunteer was wrong. (b) A voter must be registered in his own constituency; he is registered in Cuttack, not here. (c) Every adult citizen gets one vote and all votes have equal value, so no one, however much land he owns, gets two. (d) Yes: she will be 18, and old enough, for months before that election; but she must be registered as a voter in her own constituency before she can exercise the right.
s: Part (a): Entry 2, no voting on another's behalf
Part (b): registration in one's own constituency
Part (c): one vote each, equal value
Part (d): she will be old enough, but must register as a voter in her constituency

questions.q:
Illustrative figures for a small town in Karnataka in 1987: 38,500 citizens were aged 21 and above, and 4,200 citizens were aged 18 to 20. Assume every citizen aged 21 and above was registered as a voter in the town.
(a) How many citizens of the town could vote under the voting age India used before 1988?
(b) How many were of voting age once the change of 1988 came in (same population)?
(c) By what percentage did the number of people of voting age rise? Give one decimal place.
(d) Suppose, only as an assumption, that the 18-to-20 group stayed away at the same rate as the 34 per cent of eligible voters who did not vote in 2024. How many of the 4,200 would vote, and does the 'rise' in (c) therefore tell you how many extra votes were cast?
questions.a: (a) 38,500. (b) 38,500 + 4,200 = 42,700. (c) 4,200 / 38,500 x 100 = 10.9 per cent. (d) 34 per cent of 4,200 = 1,428 would stay away, so 4,200 - 1,428 = 2,772 would vote. The rise in (c) counts people who gained the right, not votes cast, so it overstates the extra votes.
s: Part (a): 38,500 under the age-21 rule
Part (b): 42,700 after the age was lowered to 18
Part (c): rise of 10.9 per cent
Part (d): 2,772 would vote; the rise counts the right, not votes cast

questions.q: Four people reach a polling booth in Bhopal on election day. By the rules this chapter states for using the right to vote, which one of them may cast a vote there?
questions.a: Asha, 19, a citizen registered as a voter in this constituency
o: Asha, 19, a citizen registered as a voter in this constituency
Bimal, 45, a citizen whose name is on the voter list in Indore
Chitra, 17, a citizen whose parents are both registered here
Dev, 30, a citizen carrying his sick brother's voter card

questions.q: Kabir says: 'Under Article 326, my city councillor, my MLA and the Vice President are all elected on the basis of universal franchise.' Test his claim and give your verdict with reasons.
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter says Article 326 bases elections to the Lok Sabha, the legislative assembly of every state and union territory, and all local elections in villages and cities on universal franchise, so the councillor and the MLA are covered. The Vice President is not: he is elected by an electoral college of the elected and nominated members of both Houses of Parliament, not by the people.
s: Verdict: partly right
Councillor and MLA are covered by the Article 326 list
The Vice President is chosen by an electoral college of MPs, not by universal franchise

questions.q: Tanvi, 20, tells her friends: 'Thanks to universal adult franchise, I will now vote for my Lok Sabha MP, my MLA, my city councillor and my state's Rajya Sabha members.' Which one of these will she NOT choose with her own vote?
questions.a: Her state's Rajya Sabha members
o: Her state's Rajya Sabha members
Her Lok Sabha MP
Her MLA in the state assembly
Her councillor in the city's municipal body

questions.q:
A student says: 'Before 1988 the minimum voting age was 21, so India's franchise could not have been universal until then.'
(a) Is the student right about the age before 1988? (b) Does the age rule alone make the franchise non-universal? Explain using what the chapter says 'universal' means.
questions.a: (a) Yes: the chapter says the minimum age was changed from 21 to 18 in 1988. (b) No. 'Universal' means that no adult citizen is left out because of caste, creed, race, religion, gender, education or income, and that every vote has equal value. An age limit applies to every citizen alike and is not one of those grounds, which is why the chapter says the Constitution makers made universal adult franchise a feature right from the outset.
s: Part (a): the age was 21 until it was changed to 18 in 1988
Part (b): an age limit applies to all alike and is not a ground of exclusion; the franchise was universal from the outset

questions.q:
(a) Kamala, 82, is unwell on polling day and asks her grandson to go to the booth and cast her vote for her. Is this allowed? Give the rule.
(b) Name the facility the chapter says was offered for the first time in 2024 that could let Kamala vote herself instead.
questions.a: (a) No. The chapter says no one can vote on another's behalf. (b) Home voting: in 2024, for the first time, the elderly and people with disabilities could cast their votes from home.
s: Part (a): not allowed, because no one may vote on another's behalf
Part (b): voting from home for the elderly, first offered in 2024

questions.q: India has universal adult franchise, yet some adult citizens cannot vote in a given election. Write a short situation (three or four sentences) about a 30-year-old citizen who cannot vote at a particular booth, name the rule from the chapter your situation uses, and explain why this does not go against universal franchise.
questions.a: Sample: Imran, 30, moved from Patna to Pune last year for work. On polling day in Pune he goes to a booth, but his name is on the voter list only in Patna, so he is turned away. Rule: to exercise the right, one must be registered as a voter in one's own constituency. This is not against universal franchise: the right is still his (he has not been left out for caste, income or any such reason); the rule only decides where he uses it. (Other valid situations: a person found guilty of certain serious crimes; someone trying to vote for another.)
s: A clear situation in which a 30-year-old citizen cannot vote
The chapter's rule it rests on (registration, serious crimes or no voting on another's behalf)
Why the rule does not exclude anyone on grounds universality rules out

questions.q:
The chapter's margin defines a 'system' as a group of interconnected or interdependent elements that work together to achieve a common purpose.
(a) Name two elements of India's electoral system that the chapter describes. (b) Say what would go wrong for the common purpose, free and fair elections, if one of your two elements stopped working.
questions.a: (a) Any two, for example: the voter list on which a citizen must be registered, the Election Commission of India, the polling officers at each station, the EVM and VVPAT. (b) Elements depend on each other: if the voter list failed, citizens with the right to vote could not exercise it; if the polling officers or machines failed, the vote could not be cast or checked. The elections would then no longer be free and fair for every voter.
s: Part (a): two elements of the electoral system named from the chapter
Part (b): the failure of one element harms the common purpose because the elements depend on each other

questions.q: Before 1988 a citizen could vote only from age 21; the limit then became 18. A citizen born in 1972 turned 18 in 1990. Under the old limit she would have first voted in 1993; under the limit the chapter gives, she first became eligible in ___.
Justify the statement: 'India's franchise is universal, but it is not without conditions.' Explain what makes it universal and set out every condition or limit the chapter gives.
questions.a: Universal: every adult citizen gets one vote and all votes have equal value, irrespective of caste, creed, race, religion, gender, education or income; the Constitution makers chose this from the outset, and it covers Lok Sabha, assembly and local elections (Article 326). Conditions: the voter must be a citizen aged 18 or above (lowered from 21 in 1988); she must be registered as a voter in her own constituency; no one may vote on another's behalf; and a person found guilty of certain serious crimes is barred. None of these conditions picks out a social group, so the franchise stays universal while still having rules.
s: Universal: one vote each, equal value, no exclusion on caste, religion, gender, education or income
Coverage: Lok Sabha, assemblies and local elections under Article 326
Age and citizenship condition, with the 1988 change
Registration in one's constituency and no voting on another's behalf
Bar for serious crimes, and why the conditions do not undo universality

questions.q:
Illustrative figures for a town in Gujarat (not from the book): 10,000 residents, of whom 2,400 are under 18. All the residents are citizens. Of those aged 18 and above, 6,400 are registered as voters in their own constituency, and 200 of these registered persons have been found guilty of one of the serious crimes that bar a person from voting.
(a) How many residents are of voting age?
(b) How many of them are not registered?
(c) How many can actually cast a vote, and what percentage of the adults is that? Give one decimal place.
(d) A councillor says the 1,200 unregistered adults have been 'denied universal franchise'. Judge this, using what the chapter says is needed before one can exercise the right.
questions.a: (a) 10,000 - 2,400 = 7,600. (b) 7,600 - 6,400 = 1,200. (c) 6,400 - 200 = 6,200 can vote; 6,200 / 7,600 x 100 = 81.6 per cent of the adults. (d) The claim is wrong: the 1,200 hold the right to vote, since universal franchise is for every adult citizen; the chapter says a person must be registered as a voter in her constituency to exercise it, so what they lack is registration. Nothing in the figures shows that they were excluded for caste, gender, education or income.
s: Part (c): 6,200 voters, 81.6 per cent of adults
Part (d): the right exists; registration is the step they lack; not denied on any excluded ground

questions.q:
Match each term in Column A with the example in Column B that fits the chapter's meaning of it.
Column A: 1. Franchise  2. Constituency  3. System  4. Universal
Column B: a. the area of Lucknow whose voters together elect one representative  b. the right to vote that the Constitution grants a citizen  c. officers, voter lists, polling stations and machines working together for one purpose  d. no adult citizen left out because of caste, religion, gender or income
A teacher asks the class to list the reasons given in the chapter's mindmap for universal adult franchise. A student offers four suggestions. Which one should she strike off?
questions.a: It guarantees that every winner gets more than half the votes
o: It guarantees that every winner gets more than half the votes
It lets people vote out representatives who fail them
It makes everyone's voice count in deciding the nation's future
It lets people decide the kind of future they want

questions.q: Before a municipal election, a labour contractor tells his workers, 'Voting is for educated people; you need not bother.' Which reason in the chapter's mindmap is his remark most directly against?
questions.a: Everyone is equal: no discrimination on education
o: Everyone is equal: no discrimination on education
Universal franchise fosters civic engagement in one's own area
Elected representatives are answerable to the electorate
People get the power to decide the future they want

questions.q:
(a) What does the chapter say ensured that Indian women had voting rights from the very beginning?
(b) A classmate says, 'Indian women got the vote because they fought as long and hard as women in Switzerland.' Use the chapter to correct her.
questions.a: (a) A progressive constitutional vision and deep democratic values rooted in India's ancient traditions. (b) The chapter says women in many countries fought long and hard to win the vote (Swiss women got it only in 1971), whereas in India the Constitution gave women the vote from the very beginning, so the long struggle she describes is what the chapter says happened elsewhere.
s: Part (a): progressive constitutional vision and democratic values rooted in ancient traditions
Part (b): the long struggle was elsewhere; India's women had the vote from the beginning

questions.q:
Analyse how the chapter's reasons for universal franchise would be weakened if one half of the adult population, women, were left out of voting, as they were in Switzerland until 1971.
(a) Take four of the five reasons in the mindmap and show, for each, what would be lost.
(b) Explain why the chapter treats India's choice on women's vote as a mark of its democratic values.
questions.a: (a) Everyone is equal: there would be discrimination based on sex, which the mindmap rules out. Everyone's voice matters: half the population would have no part in deciding the nation's future. Power to determine one's future: women could not decide what future they want or who represents them. Representatives answerable to the electorate: leaders would not need to answer to women, who could not vote them out. Civic engagement: women's participation in solving problems in their area would be weakened. (Any four.) (b) The chapter says a progressive constitutional vision and deep democratic values ensured that Indian women had voting rights from the very beginning, while women in many countries had to fight long and hard; so India placed women's equality at the base of its democracy.
s: Part (a): four reasons, each with what would be lost
Part (b): India's choice shows a progressive constitutional vision and democratic values

questions.q: The answer to a quiz question is: 'the power to determine one's future'. Write a short real-life situation (two or three sentences) in which a voter in India uses universal franchise in exactly this way, then explain how your situation differs from an example of 'fosters civic engagement'.
questions.a: Sample: Lakshmi, a weaver in Varanasi, listens to every candidate's plans for handloom workers and votes for the one she thinks will best shape her family's livelihood for the coming years. Here the vote is the tool: people decide what kind of future they want and who can best represent them. Civic engagement is different: it is people themselves taking part in solving problems in their area (for example, weavers forming a group to repair their market), not only choosing who represents them.
s: A situation where a voter chooses the future she wants and who can best represent her
Link to the mindmap's meaning of the reason
Contrast with civic engagement: people solving local problems themselves

questions.q:
Illustrative: a researcher writes in her notebook, 'Before Independence around 13 per cent of Indians were allowed to vote. In 1947 about 14 per cent of Indians were literate. The two figures are almost equal, so the vote before Independence must have been given to the literate.'
(a) State what each of the two figures measures, with the year or period it belongs to.
(b) Does the chapter say who the 13 per cent were? What do you conclude about her sentence?
(c) Name the choice the Constitution makers made about literacy and the vote, although some argued otherwise.
(d) She wants to print her conclusion as a fact in a school report. Judge this, and write one sentence she could safely print using only the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 13 per cent: the share of Indians who were allowed to vote before Independence, when franchise was not universal. 14 per cent: the overall literacy rate in 1947 (about 8 per cent among women). (b) No: the chapter does not say who the 13 per cent were. The two figures measure different things (permission to vote, ability to read) in different periods, so her 'must have' is a guess, not something the chapter supports. (c) They chose universal franchise from the outset, so the vote did not depend on being literate, though some argued it should go only to the literate. (d) She should not print it as a fact. A safe sentence: 'Before Independence only around 13 per cent of Indians were allowed to vote and franchise was not universal; in 1947 the literacy rate was about 14 per cent, and the Constitution makers still chose universal franchise.'
s: Part (a): 13 per cent allowed to vote before Independence; 14 per cent literate in 1947
Part (b): the chapter does not say who they were; different measures, so her inference is unsupported
Part (c): universal franchise from the outset without a literacy condition
Part (d): not printable as fact; a safe sentence using only the chapter

questions.q: Differentiate between two reasons in the chapter's mindmap, 'Everyone is equal' and 'Everyone's voice matters', with one example of each.
questions.a: 'Everyone is equal' is about no discrimination: caste, creed, sex, education or wealth make no difference to the vote (for example, a labourer and a factory owner each get one vote). 'Everyone's voice matters' is about taking part: all can participate in deciding the nation's future (for example, voters in a remote hamlet help choose the Lok Sabha just as city voters do).
s: Everyone is equal: no discrimination by caste, creed, sex, education or wealth, with an example
Everyone's voice matters: all take part in deciding the nation's future, with an example

questions.q:
In 1947 some people argued that the right to vote should be given only to literate people. Evaluate this argument.
(a) Using the literacy figures the chapter gives for 1947, work out what share of all Indians, and what share of women, a literate-only vote would have shut out.
(b) Explain how such a rule would have clashed with three different reasons for universal franchise in the chapter's mindmap.
(c) Give your final judgement on the Constitution makers' choice.
questions.a: (a) Literacy was about 14 per cent overall and about 8 per cent among women, so about 86 per cent of Indians and about 92 per cent of women would have been shut out. (b) Everyone is equal: the rule would discriminate by education, which the mindmap rules out. Everyone's voice matters: most people would have had no part in deciding the nation's future. Representatives answerable to the electorate: leaders would answer only to a small literate group, not to the whole people. (Power to determine one's future or civic engagement are also valid.) (c) The choice of universal franchise from the outset was the sounder one: it put faith in the common citizen rather than in a test that would have left out most of the country, and most women in particular.
s: Part (a): about 86 per cent of all and 92 per cent of women shut out
Part (b): clash with three different mindmap reasons, explained
Part (c): a reasoned final judgement

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Women in India won the vote only after a long struggle, as women in Switzerland did.
Reason (R): Women in Switzerland were given the right to vote only in 1971.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
Compare the position of Indian voters before Independence with their position under the Constitution, and analyse what changed.
(a) State the share of Indians who could vote before Independence and whether franchise was universal.
(b) State what the Constitution makers decided, and give the age limit then and the change of 1988.
(c) Analyse how the change met three reasons for universal franchise given in the chapter's mindmap.
questions.a: (a) Around 13 per cent of Indians were allowed to vote, and franchise was not universal. (b) The Constitution makers made universal adult franchise a feature of democracy from the outset: every adult citizen one vote, all votes of equal value, irrespective of caste, creed, race, religion, gender, education or income. The age limit was 21, lowered to 18 in 1988. (c) Everyone is equal: no group shut out by wealth, sex or education. Everyone's voice matters: all adults, not about 13 per cent, take part in deciding the nation's future. Representatives answerable to the electorate: leaders now face the whole adult population, who can vote them out. (Power to determine one's future and civic engagement are also valid.)
s: Part (a): about 13 per cent, not universal
Part (b): universal adult franchise from the outset; 21 then, 18 from 1988
Part (c): three mindmap reasons applied to the change

questions.q:
In November 1949, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar said India had adopted adult franchise 'with an abundant faith in the common man' and that never before had 'such an experiment been so boldly undertaken'.
(a) What was the 'experiment' he was speaking of?
(b) Give one fact from the chapter that shows why it could be called bold.
questions.a: (a) Giving every adult citizen one vote of equal value from the very start of the Republic, that is, universal adult franchise. (b) Any one: only about 13 per cent of Indians could vote before Independence; literacy in 1947 was about 14 per cent overall and about 8 per cent among women, yet no literacy condition was set.
s: Part (a): universal adult franchise from the outset
Part (b): one supporting fact (13 per cent before Independence, or the low literacy figures)

questions.q: For five years the MLA of a constituency near Madurai ignored repeated complaints about flooded streets. At the next election, most voters chose a different candidate and the MLA lost. Which reason from the chapter's mindmap for universal adult franchise does this show most directly?
questions.a: Elected representatives are answerable to the electorate
o: Elected representatives are answerable to the electorate
Everyone's voice matters in deciding the nation's future
Universal franchise fosters civic engagement among people
Everyone is equal, with no discrimination based on wealth

questions.q:
The chapter shows a polling station set up for a single woman voter.
(a) Which reason in the mindmap says that all can participate in deciding the nation's future?
(b) Explain why arranging a whole polling station for one voter serves that reason.
questions.a: (a) Everyone's voice matters. (b) If even one eligible voter is left without a way to vote, her voice is missing; setting up a station for one person shows that every voter counts in deciding the nation's future, not only voters who are easy to reach.
s: Part (a): everyone's voice matters
Part (b): no voter is left out, so even one voice is counted

questions.q: Farmers in a district of Vidarbha compare the candidates' plans for irrigation and crop prices, then vote for the one whose plan they think will shape the next five years best for them. Which reason from the chapter's mindmap fits this most closely?
questions.a: Power to determine one's own future
o: Power to determine one's own future
Fosters civic engagement in the area
Everyone is equal before the ballot
Women vote from the very beginning

questions.q:
Read the statements about India's record on the vote.
1. Before Independence, franchise in India was universal, though only about 13 per cent of people chose to use it.
2. In 1947, about 8 per cent of women were literate, against about 14 per cent of the whole population.
3. The chapter's mindmap links 'Everyone is equal' to no discrimination based on caste, creed, sex, education or wealth.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Take the first general elections of 1951 as the first time Indian women voted. A Swiss exchange student in Bengaluru says her great-grandmother first voted in 1971, the year Swiss women were given the vote. About how many years after Indian women first voted was that?
questions.a: About 20 years
o: About 20 years
About 34 years
About 17 years
About 24 years

questions.q: True or False? 'In 1947 literacy among Indian women was lower than the literacy of the population as a whole, yet Indian women received the right to vote from the very beginning, along with men.' Give the verdict and the evidence.
questions.a: True. Literacy in 1947 was about 14 per cent overall and only about 8 per cent among women, but the Constitution chose universal adult franchise from the outset and the chapter says Indian women had voting rights from the very beginning.
s: Verdict: True
Evidence: 8 per cent against 14 per cent literacy, and women's vote from the very beginning

questions.q: Arjun says: 'The chapter gives only one reason for universal franchise, that it treats every voter as equal, and it gives no other.' Test his claim and give your verdict with reasons.
questions.a: No. 'Everyone is equal', meaning no discrimination based on caste, creed, sex, education or wealth, is one reason in the chapter's mindmap, but the mindmap gives four more: the power to determine one's future, everyone's voice mattering in deciding the nation's future, elected representatives being answerable to the electorate, and fostering civic engagement. The chapter even invites students to add reasons of their own.
s: Verdict: no
Equality is one reason, but only one of five
At least two of the other reasons named

questions.q:
Illustrative case: a housing society in Jaipur has 240 households, 150 of owners and 90 of tenants. Every household, owner or tenant, pays the same maintenance of Rs 1,800 a month. At the last committee election only owners voted: 100 owner households voted for the sitting committee and 50 against. The committee then turned down a request to repair the lift in Block C, where 60 of the 90 rented flats are. For the next election, Proposal X keeps the vote for owners only; Proposal Y gives one vote to every household. (Assume one vote per household.)
(a) Under Proposal X, what percentage of households would have no say in choosing the committee?
(b) Which reason from the chapter's mindmap, about what elected representatives owe to those who vote for them, did the lift decision show was missing?
(c) Owners say they have more at stake because they own the flats. Which fact in the case weakens this argument?
(d) Predict what happens to the sitting committee under each proposal if every voter votes as before and all 90 tenant households vote against it.
questions.a: (a) 90 / 240 x 100 = 37.5 per cent. (b) Elected representatives answerable to the electorate: the committee did not have to answer to the tenants, so it could ignore their lift. (c) Tenants pay exactly the same Rs 1,800 maintenance and use the same lift, so they bear the same costs. (d) Under X: 100 households for and 50 against, so the committee stays. Under Y: 100 for and 50 + 90 = 140 against, so the committee is voted out. Only under Y can all the households it serves vote it out.
s: Part (a): 37.5 per cent
Part (b): answerability of representatives to the electorate
Part (c): tenants pay the same maintenance and use the same lift
Part (d): X keeps it (100 to 50); Y removes it (100 to 140)

questions.q: For years a village in Jharkhand has had a broken road to its school. Show how THREE different reasons for universal franchise in the chapter's mindmap could each help the villagers get the road repaired. Name each reason and say what the villagers would do.
questions.a: Power to determine one's future: they vote for the candidate whose plan for roads and schooling they trust. Elected representatives answerable to the electorate: if the representative ignores the road, they can vote her out next time. Fosters civic engagement: villagers form a group, list the damaged stretches and take the problem to their panchayat and representative. (Everyone is equal or everyone's voice matters, applied correctly, are also accepted.)
s: First reason named with a matching action
Second reason named with a matching action
Third reason named with a matching action

questions.q: Before Independence, the chapter says, around 13 per cent of Indians were allowed to vote. At that rate, in an illustrative group of 500 Indians of that time, about ___ would have been allowed to vote.
True or False? 'If every eligible voter who stayed away in 2024 had voted, the number of voters would have risen by about half.' Give the verdict and the working.
questions.a: True. About 34 per cent did not vote, so about 66 per cent did. If the 34 had joined the 66, the voters would have risen by 34 / 66 = about 51.5 per cent, which is about half.
s: Verdict: True
Working: 34 / 66 is about 51.5 per cent, close to half

questions.q:
Read the statements about the scale of Indian elections and the efforts to reach voters.
1. In 2024, for the first time, the elderly and persons with disabilities could cast their votes from home.
2. The comparison with France is about area, while the comparison with the United Kingdom is about the number of people.
3. Over 968 million voters were eligible to vote for the 543 constituencies of the Lok Sabha in 2024.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q: A newspaper notes that India is about six times larger in area than France. Which difficulty of running Indian elections does THIS comparison point to?
questions.a: Reaching voters spread over a vast, varied land
o: Reaching voters spread over a vast, varied land
Serving the sheer number of eligible voters at once
Persuading the 34 per cent who stayed away
Counting the votes of 968 million people

questions.q:
(a) Give one reason why an eligible voter might not vote that one of the chapter's accessibility measures could remove, and name that measure.
(b) Give one reason the chapter itself names as a challenge, which no such measure can remove.
questions.a: (a) For example: an elderly or disabled voter who cannot reach the booth (home voting); a voter in a remote place (officials travel there); a wheelchair user facing steps (app-based request for a wheelchair or ramp); a visually impaired voter (braille-enabled voter card). (b) Voter apathy, especially in urban areas: some people are able to vote but choose not to, which needs awareness, not access.
s: Part (a): an access barrier matched to the right measure
Part (b): voter apathy, which needs awareness rather than access

questions.q:
The chapter says India has 3.1 million elected representatives, 1.3 million of them women, in more than 250,000 local government bodies.
(a) How many of these representatives are men?
(b) What does the chapter say about how all of them are chosen, and what does that show about how far universal franchise reaches?
questions.a: (a) 3.1 - 1.3 = 1.8 million. (b) All of them are democratically elected through universal adult franchise, so the same one-person-one-vote right that elects the Lok Sabha also reaches every village and city local body.
s: Part (a): 1.8 million
Part (b): elected through universal adult franchise, reaching local bodies too

questions.q:
Illustrative figures for one district: 12,000 registered voters are either elderly or persons with disabilities. At the previous general election, before the 2024 measure the chapter describes, 3,000 of them voted. In 2024, 5,400 of them voted from home and 1,800 voted at polling stations.
(a) What percentage of this group voted at the previous election?
(b) What percentage voted in 2024?
(c) Which measure from the chapter best explains the change, and what was new about it in 2024?
(d) An official writes: 'The 4,800 who still did not vote in 2024 all stayed away because they could not reach a booth.' Judge whether these figures support his statement.
questions.a: (a) 3,000 / 12,000 = 25 per cent. (b) (5,400 + 1,800) / 12,000 = 7,200 / 12,000 = 60 per cent. (c) Voting from home: in 2024, for the first time, the elderly and persons with disabilities could cast their votes from home; 5,400 of the 7,200 used it. (d) Not supported. The figures show how many did not vote (12,000 - 7,200 = 4,800) but not why; since home voting was available to this whole group, some may have stayed away for other reasons, such as lack of interest. A survey would be needed to know.
s: Part (a): 25 per cent
Part (b): 60 per cent
Part (c): home voting, offered for the first time in 2024
Part (d): not supported; the data give the number, not the reason

questions.q:
A student news blog published this report after the 2024 general election:
'Over 968 million voters were eligible for the 543 Lok Sabha constituencies. Our country is fifteen times larger in area than France. For the first time, home voting was offered to every voter in the country. Turnout was about 34 per cent.'
(a) Correct the comparison with France, and say which country and which measure the number fifteen actually belongs to.
(b) Correct the sentence on home voting.
(c) Correct the turnout sentence.
(d) Suppose the share of eligible voters who did not vote had been 20 per cent instead of 34 per cent, with the same 968 million eligible. How many more million voters would have voted? Give two decimal places.
questions.a: (a) India is six times larger in area than France; fifteen is the comparison with the United Kingdom, whose population India's eligible voters exceed fifteen times. (b) Home voting was offered to the elderly and persons with disabilities, not to every voter. (c) About 34 per cent of eligible voters did NOT vote, so turnout was about 66 per cent. (d) 14 per cent of 968 million = 135.52 million more voters (turnout would have been 80 per cent instead of 66).
s: Part (a): six times France in area; fifteen is the UK population comparison
Part (b): home voting for the elderly and persons with disabilities only
Part (c): 34 per cent did not vote; turnout about 66 per cent
Part (d): 135.52 million more voters

questions.q: The chapter says India needs 'an elaborate and well-organised system' to run its elections. Give three reasons for this, each backed by a different fact or figure from the chapter.
questions.a: Size: over 968 million eligible voters in 2024, fifteen times the UK's population. Spread: 543 constituencies over a country six times the area of France, with difficult geography, so officials must travel to remote places. Inclusion: the system must reach the elderly, persons with disabilities and other voters with special needs (home voting, braille voter cards, wheelchairs and ramps). (The 3.1 million local representatives in over 250,000 bodies are also a valid figure.)
s: Size of the electorate with a figure
Area or geographic diversity with a figure
Inclusion of voters with special needs with an example

questions.q:
In 2024, over 968 million voters were eligible for the 543 Lok Sabha constituencies.
(a) On average, about how many eligible voters did one constituency have? Give the answer in millions to two decimal places.
(b) If about 34 per cent of the voters of such an average constituency stayed away, about how many million would that be?
questions.a: (a) 968 / 543 = about 1.78 million eligible voters per constituency. (b) 1.78 x 0.34 = about 0.61 million (about 6 lakh) voters.
s: Part (a): about 1.78 million
Part (b): about 0.61 million

questions.q: Justify the statement: 'Running a general election in India is a challenge of size, spread and inclusion.' Give figures for size, a comparison for spread, and at least three measures the Election Commission used for inclusion.
questions.a: Size: over 968 million voters were eligible in 2024 for 543 Lok Sabha constituencies; India's eligible voters are fifteen times the UK's population. Spread: India is six times the area of France and its geographic diversity is itself a challenge, so electoral officials travel to remote locations. Inclusion: in 2024, for the first time, the elderly and persons with disabilities could vote from home; postal voting was available for a specific category of voters; braille-enabled voter cards and app-based requests for wheelchairs and ramps were made possible. Even so about 34 per cent did not vote, which shows the task is not finished.
s: Size: 968 million voters, 543 constituencies or the UK comparison
Spread: the France comparison and geographic diversity
Inclusion: three ECI measures
Link to the remaining gap of 34 per cent non-voters

questions.q: At a seminar a speaker claims that women are only a tiny fraction of India's elected representatives in local government. Which figure from the chapter answers him?
questions.a: About 42 per cent: 1.3 of 3.1 million
o: About 42 per cent: 1.3 of 3.1 million
About 13 per cent, as before Independence
About 34 per cent, as in the 2024 turnout gap
About 8 per cent, as in women's literacy in 1947

questions.q: A report states: 'In 2024, every eligible voter in India cast a vote by going to a polling station.' Show that this cannot be true, using three separate facts from the chapter.
questions.a: First, about 34 per cent of eligible voters did not vote at all. Second, in 2024 the elderly and persons with disabilities could cast their votes from home. Third, a postal voting option was available for a specific category of voters. Any one fact breaks 'every'; together they show the statement cannot hold.
s: About 34 per cent did not vote
Home voting for the elderly and persons with disabilities in 2024
Postal voting for a specific category

questions.q: Ramesh says: 'About 34 per cent of eligible voters did not vote in 2024, so universal franchise did not apply to them that year.' Test his claim and give your verdict with reasons.
questions.a: No. Universal franchise is the right to vote; every eligible citizen still held it in 2024 whether or not she used it. The chapter treats non-voting as a separate problem, asking why people do not vote and what challenges they face, and it names voter apathy as a challenge. The ECI's measures (home voting, travel to remote places, braille cards) aim to help people use the right they already have.
s: Verdict: no
The right exists whether or not it is used
Non-voting is a separate challenge (apathy, barriers) the chapter asks us to address

questions.q: The chapter says India's population of eligible voters is fifteen times the population of the United Kingdom. Taking India's eligible voters as 968 million, about how large does this make the UK's population?
questions.a: About 65 million
o: About 65 million
About 161 million
About 953 million
About 145 million

questions.q: A neighbour says letting persons with disabilities vote from home is 'a special favour, not a right'. Using the meaning of universal adult franchise, give two reasons why the chapter sees such measures differently.
questions.a: Universal franchise means every adult citizen has the right to vote and all votes have equal value; a person with a disability already has this right, so the measure only removes a barrier to using it. The chapter says the ECI's measures are meant to ensure that no voter is left behind and that every eligible citizen can participate freely and fairly; without them, her equal vote would exist only on paper.
s: She already has the right; the measure removes a barrier, not grants a favour
The aim is that no voter is left behind and every voter takes part equally

questions.q: Differentiate between a barrier of 'scale' and a barrier of 'access' in Indian elections, giving one example of each from the chapter.
questions.a: A barrier of scale comes from the size of the whole exercise: over 968 million eligible voters, fifteen times the UK's population, in a country six times the area of France. A barrier of access stops a particular voter from using her vote: an elderly or disabled voter who cannot reach the booth, or a voter in a remote place, which the ECI meets with home voting or officials travelling there.
s: Scale: the size and spread of the electorate, with a figure
Access: a barrier to an individual voter, with an example

questions.q:
Illustrative survey: a Class 8 group asked 200 adults in their ward who did not vote in 2024 why they stayed away. Answers: 'the polling station was too far from our hamlet' 60; 'too old or ill to go' 50; 'disability made the booth hard to use' 30; 'not interested' 60.
(a) Work out the percentage for each reason.
(b) For each of the first three reasons, name a measure from the chapter that answers it.
(c) Which reason is not answered by any accessibility measure? Name the challenge the chapter gives for it and propose two steps the chapter's 'road ahead' supports.
questions.a: (a) 60/200 = 30 per cent; 50/200 = 25 per cent; 30/200 = 15 per cent; 60/200 = 30 per cent. (b) Too far: electoral officials travel to remote locations to set up voting. Old or ill: voting from home (offered to the elderly from 2024). Disability: home voting, braille-enabled voter cards or app-based requests for wheelchairs and ramps. (c) 'Not interested' (30 per cent): voter apathy, which the chapter names as a challenge, especially in urban areas. Steps: awareness campaigns through media and education, especially for the youth; giving voters the information they need to make responsible choices.
s: Part (a): 30, 25, 15 and 30 per cent
Part (b): a correct measure for each of the three access reasons
Part (c): voter apathy named, with two steps from the road ahead

questions.q: The chapter says India has 3.1 million elected representatives in more than 250,000 local government bodies. Taking the number of bodies as 250,000, about how many elected representatives does each body have on average?
questions.a: About 12
o: About 12
About 124
About 81
About 1.2

questions.q: About 34 per cent of eligible voters did not vote in 2024. If a polling booth with 1,250 eligible voters matched this national figure exactly, ___ of its voters would have stayed away.
A district election officer sorts the chapter's accessibility measures by who they help. Which measure helps voters because of WHERE they live, and not because of their age or a disability?
questions.a: Electoral officials travelling to remote locations
o: Electoral officials travelling to remote locations
Voting from home for the elderly and persons with disabilities
Braille-enabled voter cards
App-based requests for a wheelchair or ramp

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Electoral officials travel to remote locations so that every citizen there can exercise the right to vote.
Reason (R): India sets up a polling station only where a large number of voters live, and never for a single voter. (The caption of the chapter's Fig. 5.6 mentions a polling station organised for a single woman voter.)
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: On polling day a booth officer meets three voters: Sunita, who uses a wheelchair and finds the entrance steep; Imran, who cannot read printed voter cards; and Mrs Bose, 91, who cannot leave her bed. Which set of the chapter's measures matches the three, in that order?
questions.a: An app request for a ramp; a braille-enabled voter card; voting from home
o: An app request for a ramp; a braille-enabled voter card; voting from home
Voting from home; an app request for a ramp; a braille-enabled voter card
A braille-enabled voter card; voting from home; officials travelling to a remote place
Postal voting; a braille-enabled voter card; an app request for a wheelchair

questions.q:
Illustrative: in a class of 36, 14 students leave their ballot papers unmarked. The rest vote: Asha 9, Bilal 8, Chetan 5.
(a) Who is elected, and what share of the whole class voted for the winner?
(b) Give one problem this creates for the new representative.
(c) Suggest how the unhappy students could have shown their view more usefully, using an option from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Asha, with the most votes (9); 9 / 36 = 25 per cent of the class. (b) She speaks for the class but only a quarter chose her, so her support is weak and many classmates may not back her plans. (c) Choosing NOTA, if offered, records a deliberate rejection of all candidates and sends the message that voters want better choices, whereas an unmarked paper is simply invalid.
s: Part (a): Asha, 25 per cent of the class
Part (b): weak support for the representative
Part (c): NOTA records rejection; an unmarked paper is only invalid

questions.q: A class of 30 casts all 30 ballots. The count reads: Dev 10, Eva 9, NOTA 5 and 6 ballot papers with no mark at all. Which statement fits the Suryodaya caselet and the chapter's box on NOTA?
questions.a: Dev is elected; the unmarked ballots are invalid and NOTA does not change the result
o: Dev is elected; the unmarked ballots are invalid and NOTA does not change the result
Eva is elected, because Dev has fewer than half of the 30 ballots cast in all
NOTA wins, because the 5 NOTA and 6 unmarked ballots together exceed Dev's 10
No one is elected, because the unmarked ballots are more than Dev's margin

questions.q: Kavya says: 'The 10th-century Uttaramerur selection and the Suryodaya class election both had steps meant to make people trust the result, even though one used chance and the other used votes.' Test her claim and give your verdict with evidence from both.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. Uttaramerur: names on palm leaves were sealed in a pot, the pot was opened publicly, a young boy drew the leaves at random and a respected man showed his empty hands before reading each name. Suryodaya: an Election Officer explained the rules, voting was by secret ballot, the box was sealed until counting and a teacher from the next class witnessed the count. The method differed (random draw against counting votes), but both made the process transparent.
s: Verdict: yes
Trust-building steps at Uttaramerur
Trust-building steps at Suryodaya, and the difference of chance and votes

questions.q: A school in Indore wants to save time by electing its class representatives with a show of hands instead of the secret ballot used at Suryodaya. Evaluate the idea: give one thing it would gain, two things it would lose, and your judgement.
questions.a: Gain: it is quicker, needing no ballot papers, booth or sealed box. Loss 1: everyone would see whom each student chose, so friends or the candidates could pressure voters; the secret ballot keeps the vote private and fair. Loss 2: with no ballots in a box sealed until the counting session, there is nothing for a witness like Ms Sheeba to see counted afterwards. Judgement: the time saved is small compared with losing a free and fair choice, so the secret ballot should stay.
s: One gain: speed
Two losses: pressure without secrecy; no sealed ballots for a witnessed count
Judgement that the secret ballot should stay

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Suryodaya election and NOTA.
1. Every student could see whom each classmate voted for, which made the result transparent.
2. Ms Usha arranged a ballot paper in braille for Neha.
3. NOTA changes the result if it gets more votes than any candidate.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 only
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: In a Lok Sabha constituency (illustrative figures): Candidate P 40,000 votes, Candidate Q 38,000 and NOTA 9,000. A student says that NOTA's 9,000 is more than P's lead of 2,000, so the election must be cancelled. What does the chapter say about NOTA?
questions.a: P still wins; NOTA cannot change the result but signals a wish for better choices
o: P still wins; NOTA cannot change the result but signals a wish for better choices
The poll is repeated, because NOTA's 9,000 votes beat the winning margin
Q wins, because NOTA votes are added to the runner-up's total
NOTA ballots are invalid and are ignored completely in the count

questions.q: In the 10th-century Uttaramerur process, which step did the same job as Ms Usha sealing the ballot box until the counting session?
questions.a: Sealing the pot of palm leaves till selection day
o: Sealing the pot of palm leaves till selection day
A young boy drawing the palm leaves out one by one
A respected man first showing his empty hands
Reading out each selected name to the public

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Gurmat was elected Class Representative with fewer than half of all the votes cast.
Reason (R): Whoever gets the most votes wins; the winner need not have half of the votes.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Three candidates at Suryodaya each used a different way to campaign and spoke for a different promise. Which candidate is correctly paired with BOTH a campaign method and the promise from the caselet?
questions.a: Ravi: a lunchtime music performance, for more arts time
o: Ravi: a lunchtime music performance, for more arts time
Ahmed: a lunchtime music performance, for cleaner classrooms
Gurmat: posters, for peer coaching and mutual support
Ravi: talks at the noticeboard, for more time for the arts

questions.q: At the Suryodaya count, Gurmat received 12 votes, Ravi 10 and Ahmed 8, and one ballot was invalid. Gurmat's lead over the runner-up was ___ votes.

In a residents' association election in Mysuru, members are asked to raise their hands for their candidate while everyone watches. Which feature of the Suryodaya election does this method give up, whatever else is in place?
questions.a: The secret ballot
o: The secret ballot
An outside witness
A braille ballot
An Election Officer

questions.q:
(a) Why did Ms Usha arrange a ballot paper in braille for Neha?
(b) Which idea about universal franchise from earlier in the chapter does this small step put into practice?
questions.a: (a) So that Neha, who reads braille, could read the names and mark her vote herself, in secret, like everyone else. (b) That every eligible voter must be able to take part and no voter is left behind (everyone's voice matters, everyone is equal); it mirrors the ECI's braille-enabled voter cards.
s: Part (a): so Neha could read and mark her own ballot privately
Part (b): no voter left behind / everyone's voice matters, as with braille voter cards

questions.q: In the Suryodaya caselet, Ms Usha called Ms Sheeba from the next class before counting began. What did this step add to the election?
questions.a: Someone outside the class saw the count done fairly
o: Someone outside the class saw the count done fairly
A second Election Officer to replace Ms Usha that day
A teacher who would decide which ballots were invalid
An extra vote to break any tie between the candidates

questions.q: Differentiate between an invalid ballot and a NOTA vote, using the Suryodaya caselet and the chapter's box on NOTA.
questions.a: An invalid ballot is one that cannot be counted for anyone, like the Suryodaya ballot that was not marked at all; it shows no choice. A NOTA vote is a deliberate choice of 'None Of The Above': the voter rejects all candidates, it is recorded, and while it does not change the result it sends the message that voters want better choices.
s: Invalid ballot: unmarked, shows no choice, not counted
NOTA: a deliberate, recorded rejection of all candidates that sends a message

questions.q:
Match each step of the Suryodaya election in Column A with the problem it guards against in Column B.
Column A: 1. Secret ballot  2. Election Officer explaining the rules  3. Sealing the ballot box  4. A witness from the next class
Column B: a. ballots being added or removed after voting closes  b. voters being pressured because others can see their choice  c. no one outside the class being able to confirm the count was honest  d. students voting without knowing how the process works

(a) Name two things the chapter says the Class Rep would do at Suryodaya.
(b) Ravi promised more room for the arts in the class timetable. Using the Class Rep's role, explain why the class needs a representative to turn such a promise into action.
questions.a: (a) Any two: represent the class in meetings with teachers, organise events, act as a bridge between the students and school authorities. (b) A promise about the timetable is something to be put to the teachers and school authorities; the Class Rep is the person who meets them on the class's behalf and acts as the bridge, so the winning candidate's promise reaches those who can act on it.
s: Part (a): two roles from the caselet
Part (b): the representative carries the class's request to teachers and school authorities

questions.q:
Illustrative case: a school hostel in Hyderabad elects a mess committee head. Two notes about the election survive.
Note 1, by the winner's roommate: 'Swathi won by a huge margin. Everyone backed her openly at lunch, and we all knew how the others voted.'
Note 2, by a teacher from another hostel who witnessed the count: 'Ballots were marked in a booth and dropped in a sealed box. 42 ballots: Swathi 19, Divya 17, NOTA 4, unmarked 2.'
(a) What percentage of the 42 ballots went to Swathi? Give one decimal place.
(b) Is 'a huge margin' supported by Note 2?
(c) Which detail in Note 1 clashes with the voting method described in Note 2?
(d) Compare the winning margin with the number of NOTA ballots. Does the chapter let the NOTA ballots change the result, and what do they signal?
questions.a: (a) 19 / 42 x 100 = 45.2 per cent. (b) No: Swathi led Divya by only 2 votes (19 against 17). (c) 'We all knew how the others voted' clashes with the secret ballot in a booth; with a secret ballot no one knows who voted for whom. (d) The margin is 2 votes and there are 4 NOTA ballots, twice as many. The chapter says NOTA does not change the result, so Swathi is still elected, but those 4 ballots signal that voters want better choices.
s: Part (a): 45.2 per cent
Part (b): not supported; the margin was 2 votes
Part (c): knowing others' votes clashes with the secret ballot
Part (d): margin 2 against 4 NOTA ballots; the result stands and NOTA signals a wish for better choices

questions.q: Give two reasons why the class teacher, rather than one of the candidates or their friends, was a sensible choice as Election Officer in the Suryodaya election.
questions.a: First, she was not contesting, so she had no reason to favour Ahmed, Gurmat or Ravi; the chapter says she was appointed to ensure the process was fair and transparent. Second, she had to organise the polls, explain the rules and see that all the necessary rules were followed, a job that needs someone every candidate trusts.
s: She had no stake in the result, so she could be fair
Her job was to organise, explain and enforce the rules, which needs everyone's trust

questions.q:
Illustrative case: Class 7B of a school in Guwahati elects its class representative. 38 students are present and 38 ballot papers are handed out. The ballot paper also has a NOTA box. After voting, the Election Officer seals the box; at the count, which a teacher from another class witnesses, the tally reads: Riya 15, Tenzin 13, Arif 6, NOTA 2, unmarked 1.
(a) How many ballot papers were found in the box?
(b) What does this total reveal, and which step of the Suryodaya process lets someone from outside the class check the figures?
(c) Who wins, and does the NOTA count affect the result?
(d) Can the missing ballot paper change who wins? Show it with the figures.
questions.a: (a) 15 + 13 + 6 + 2 + 1 = 37. (b) One of the 38 ballot papers handed out is not in the box. The witness from another class, who sees the count, can check the figures against the number issued. (c) Riya wins with the most votes, 15; NOTA does not change the result. (d) No. Riya leads Tenzin by 2. If the missing paper were a vote for Tenzin, he would have 14, still fewer than her 15, so the winner stays the same.
s: Part (a): 37 ballots
Part (b): one ballot missing; the outside witness can check the figures
Part (c): Riya wins; NOTA does not change the result
Part (d): Riya 15 against at most 14 for Tenzin, so the result stands

questions.a: (a) Ms Usha, the class teacher, was appointed Election Officer and explained the rules, so the process was organised by someone neutral and every student knew how to vote. (b) Booths in a corner and the secret ballot meant no one knew who voted for whom, so no one could be pressured. (c) A braille ballot for Neha let her vote on her own and in secret, so no voter was left out. (d) The box was sealed until counting and Ms Sheeba from the next class witnessed the count, so ballots could not be changed and the result could be trusted by all. (e) The unmarked ballot was declared invalid, so no one could claim it for any candidate.
s: Part (a): neutral officer and clear rules
Part (b): secrecy prevents pressure
Part (c): braille ballot includes every voter
Part (d): seal and witness prevent tampering and doubt
Part (e): invalid ballot not claimed by anyone

questions.q: True or False? 'In the Suryodaya election, the secret ballot still allowed Ms Usha, as Election Officer, to know who had voted for whom.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Ms Usha explained that with the secret ballot no one would know who voted for whom, which kept the process private and fair; that included her, as Election Officer.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: under a secret ballot no one, including the officer, knows who voted for whom

questions.q:
Compare the 10th-century Uttaramerur process with the Suryodaya School class election.
(a) Give three ways in which both processes guarded against unfairness, pairing a step from each.
(b) Give two differences in how the representative was actually chosen or who took part.
questions.a: (a) Guarding the record: the sealed pot of palm leaves and the sealed ballot box. Public view: the pot was opened in front of the public, and the count at Suryodaya was watched by Ms Sheeba from the next class. A trusted person in charge: the respected individual who showed empty hands and read the names, and Ms Usha as Election Officer seeing that the rules were followed. (b) At Uttaramerur the representatives were picked by a random draw by a young boy, while at Suryodaya each student voted and the one with the most votes won. At Suryodaya the voters' choices were secret ballots marked with an 'X'; at Uttaramerur the people did not mark any choice, they only watched the draw.
s: Part (a): first matched pair (sealed pot and sealed box)
Part (a): second matched pair (public opening and outside witness)
Part (a): third matched pair (trusted official in charge)
Part (b): random draw against counting votes
Part (b): voters marking secret ballots against watching a draw

questions.q: True or False? 'The Election Commission of India conducts the election of the President, even though ordinary voters do not cast votes in it.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the ECI conducts elections to the offices of the President and the Vice President as well as to the Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha and assemblies. The President is chosen by an electoral college of elected representatives, not by the people, but it is still an election the ECI oversees.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the ECI conducts the President's election, which is held through an electoral college

questions.q: A week before polling in a state, a minister of the ruling party announces a new housing scheme for the district where voting is due. Which element of the Model Code of Conduct does this break?
questions.a: The rules the party in government must follow
o: The rules the party in government must follow
All candidates being expected to show discretion and restraint
Influencing voters through gifts in return for votes
None of the three elements, since a scheme is not a gift

questions.q:
(a) Name the body that manages the election to the Lok Sabha and the body that manages the election to the gram panchayats of the villages in the same district.
(b) A councillor says the body in the second case works entirely on its own. Which words of the chapter show he is wrong?
questions.a: (a) The Election Commission of India manages the Lok Sabha election; the State Election Commission manages the gram panchayat elections. (b) The chapter says the State Election Commissions work in consultation with the Election Commission of India.
s: Part (a): ECI for the Lok Sabha, State Election Commission for gram panchayats
Part (b): the State Election Commission works in consultation with the ECI

questions.q: A voter's complaint is passed up the chapter's chart of the Election Commission of India. Which order lists these three officers from the national level down to the district level?
questions.a: Chief Election Commissioner, Chief Electoral Officer, District Election Officer
o: Chief Election Commissioner, Chief Electoral Officer, District Election Officer
Chief Electoral Officer, Chief Election Commissioner, District Election Officer
District Election Officer, Chief Electoral Officer, Chief Election Commissioner
Chief Election Commissioner, District Election Officer, Chief Electoral Officer

questions.q:
Illustrative case: in one constituency in the 1980s, before voter IDs, an inquiry estimated that 2 out of every 100 votes cast had been cast by people voting in someone else's name. 1,50,000 votes were cast, and the winner's lead over the runner-up was 2,000 votes.
(a) About how many votes were cast in other people's names?
(b) Which reform of T.N. Seshan was aimed at this practice, and what is the practice called?
(c) At a polling station today, which polling officer deals with the voter's name and ID proof? (Assume that officer also checks that the ID belongs to the person standing there.)
(d) Predict whether these false votes could have decided the result, and say how many would have had to go to the winner.
questions.a: (a) 2 per cent of 1,50,000 = 3,000 votes. (b) Voter IDs, brought in to eliminate proxy voting. (c) The first polling officer, who checks the voter's name on the voter list and her ID proof (so a person using someone else's name would be stopped if the ID is matched to the person). (d) Yes, they could have: 3,000 false votes is more than the 2,000-vote lead, so if more than 2,000 of them had gone to the winner, the runner-up would really have won or tied: more than 2,000 would be needed to overturn the lead. The result cannot be trusted, which is why ending proxy voting mattered.
s: Part (a): 3,000 votes
Part (b): voter IDs to eliminate proxy voting
Part (c): the first polling officer's check of name and ID
Part (d): 3,000 exceeds the 2,000 lead, so the result could have been decided by them

questions.q:
Give the reason why each of these is treated as a violation during an election campaign:
(a) At a rally in Bihar, a candidate calls his rival abusive names from the stage.
(b) During an inspection, Rs 40 lakh in bundles of Rs 500 notes is found in a candidate's jeep.
questions.a: (a) The code expects all candidates to exercise discretion and restraint so that elections take place peacefully; abuse of a rival breaks this. (b) Such cash can be used to influence voters, for example through gifts in return for votes, which is punishable; it also goes against the strict vigilance on candidates' spending brought in by T.N. Seshan.
s: Part (a): breaks the expectation of restraint for peaceful elections
Part (b): cash can buy votes; vigilance on spending

questions.q:
Illustrative complaint log of a district election office during assembly polls in Karnataka:
Complaint 1: After the polls were announced, a minister of the ruling party opened a new water scheme in a constituency that votes next week.
Complaint 2: A candidate's supporters handed silver coins to families in a colony and asked them to vote for him.
Complaint 3: A voter found that her name was missing from the voter list.
Complaint 4: A candidate used abusive words about a rival at a rally.
(a) Which complaint concerns the rules for the party in government?
(b) Which complaint describes a practice the code calls punishable?
(c) Which complaint is not a breach of the code at all, and which officer deals with it?
(d) At the rally in Complaint 4 the rival answered in the same words. Which expectation of the code do both speeches fall short of, and does the rival's reply make the first speech acceptable?
questions.a: (a) Complaint 1. (b) Complaint 2: influencing voters through gifts in return for votes is punishable. (c) Complaint 3 is a voter-list problem, handled by the Electoral Registration Officer, who manages the voter list. (d) Both fall short of the expectation that all candidates exercise discretion and restraint so that elections take place peacefully. The expectation is placed on every candidate, so one candidate's reply does not make the other's abuse acceptable.
s: Part (a): Complaint 1
Part (b): Complaint 2, gifts for votes
Part (c): Complaint 3, Electoral Registration Officer
Part (d): the code expects discretion and restraint of all candidates; a reply does not excuse the first speech

questions.q:
A district election office receives five matters. For each, name the officer or body of the Election Commission's structure in the chapter that deals with it, and give the reason.
(a) A citizen's name is missing from the voter list.
(b) The conduct of the poll itself in a Lok Sabha constituency.
(c) Fixing the dates of the assembly elections.
(d) The election to the urban local bodies of the state.
(e) A minister of the ruling party announces a new scheme during the campaign.
questions.a: (a) The Electoral Registration Officer, who manages the voter list. (b) The Returning Officer, who conducts the election. (c) The Election Commission of India, since setting election dates is one of its tasks. (d) The State Election Commission, which manages direct elections to urban local bodies in consultation with the ECI. (e) The Election Commission of India, which enforces the Model Code of Conduct; the code bars the party in government from announcing new schemes that may influence voters.
s: Part (a): Electoral Registration Officer, voter list
Part (b): Returning Officer, conducts the election
Part (c): ECI sets election dates
Part (d): State Election Commission for urban local bodies
Part (e): ECI enforces the Model Code of Conduct

questions.q: Anil says: 'The ECI sets the election dates and registers the political parties, so it is the ECI that decides which party will form the government.' Test his claim and give your verdict with reasons.
questions.a: No. Setting dates and registering parties are among the ECI's tasks for overseeing the electoral process, so that elections are free and fair. The government is formed by the party or coalition that wins a majority of the seats in the Lok Sabha (or in the state assembly), and its leader usually becomes prime minister (or chief minister). The voters decide that through their votes; the ECI, as an independent body, only runs the process.
s: Verdict: no
The ECI's tasks are to run and oversee the process fairly
The government is formed by the party or coalition with a majority of seats, chosen by voters

questions.q:
(a) Who approved the Model Code of Conduct in Kerala in 1960, and was it forced on them?
(b) A journalist writes: 'The ECI has actively enforced the code ever since it was adopted in 1960.' Correct her, using the years 1962 and 1991.
questions.a: (a) Representatives of the major political parties of the time approved it voluntarily. (b) The ECI only circulated the code to political parties during the 1962 general elections, and became proactive in ensuring its observance from 1991.
s: Part (a): major political parties' representatives, voluntarily
Part (b): circulated in 1962; proactive enforcement only from 1991

questions.q: T.N. Seshan became Chief Election Commissioner in 1990. For each of his three reforms named in the chapter, explain what unfair practice it was meant to stop.
questions.a: Precise rules for campaigning: stopped candidates from campaigning in any way they liked, for example in ways that break the peace or misuse power. Voter IDs: stopped proxy voting, where someone votes in another person's name. Strict vigilance on candidates' spending: stopped money from being used to sway voters, such as buying votes with gifts or cash.
s: Campaign rules and what they stopped
Voter IDs to eliminate proxy voting
Vigilance on spending to stop money swaying voters

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Election Commission of India.
1. It was established in 1950, and the first general elections in independent India were held in 1951-1952.
2. It directly conducts the elections to every gram panchayat in the country.
3. At the national level it has a Chief Election Commissioner and three Election Commissioners.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
The chapter says all elections take place at different times but with some periodicity.
(a) Why does this keep the Election Commission busy every year, not just in a general election year?
(b) Why does the work need many people, such as teachers, to be deployed?
questions.a: (a) Elections to different assemblies and bodies fall due at different times, so every year several polls are held in various parts of the country based on when they are due. (b) The numbers are very large (about 968 million voters and over 1 million polling stations in 2024), so the ECI's own officers cannot run every booth; many people, including teachers, are deployed to assist.
s: Part (a): different polls fall due in different years and places
Part (b): huge numbers of voters and polling stations need extra staff such as teachers

questions.q: Write a short situation (three or four sentences) in which a voter's problem needs the Electoral Registration Officer, and a different problem on polling day needs the Returning Officer. Then explain why the two problems go to different officers.
questions.a: Sample: Farida, 19, finds on the voter list that her name is missing, so she goes to the Electoral Registration Officer of her district. On polling day, a party agent complains that the voting in her constituency is not being conducted properly, so he goes to the Returning Officer. The two go to different officers because the Electoral Registration Officer manages the voter list, while the Returning Officer conducts the election itself.
s: A voter-list problem sent to the Electoral Registration Officer
A problem in the conduct of the election sent to the Returning Officer
Reason: one manages the voter list, the other conducts the election

questions.q: Villages in a district of Tamil Nadu are about to elect their gram panchayats. Which body manages this election?
questions.a: The State Election Commission, consulting the ECI
o: The State Election Commission, consulting the ECI
The Election Commission of India, acting by itself
The Chief Electoral Officer, as the ECI's state head
The Returning Officer of the Lok Sabha constituency

questions.q: Maya says: 'The Election Commission of India conducts the elections to the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha and the state assemblies, and also to every gram panchayat.' Test her claim and give your verdict with reasons.
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter says the ECI conducts the elections to the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha and the State Legislative Assemblies (and to the offices of the President and Vice President). It does not manage the gram panchayat elections: those direct elections are managed by the State Election Commissions, working in consultation with the ECI.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha and assemblies
Wrong part: gram panchayats are managed by State Election Commissions, in consultation with the ECI

questions.q: A Class 8 student redraws the chapter's chart of the Election Commission of India and puts the officers in pairs. Which pair works at the SAME level of the chart?
questions.a: Returning Officer and Electoral Registration Officer
o: Returning Officer and Electoral Registration Officer
Chief Electoral Officer and District Election Officer
Chief Election Commissioner and Chief Electoral Officer
Election Commissioner and Returning Officer

questions.q: The Model Code of Conduct was first adopted in Kerala in 1960, and the ECI became proactive in ensuring its observance from 1991. So the code had existed for ___ years before the ECI began enforcing it proactively.

Match each situation in Column A with the officer in Column B who deals with it, as in the chapter's chart of the Election Commission.
Column A: 1. A voter in Patna finds her name missing from the voter list  2. Running the election itself in a constituency  3. Heading the Commission at the national level, with two colleagues  4. Representing the Commission at the level of the state of Bihar
Column B: a. Chief Election Commissioner  b. Electoral Registration Officer  c. Chief Electoral Officer  d. Returning Officer

(a) Meghna, a new voter in Nagpur, finds her name spelt wrongly in the voter list. Which officer in the ECI's structure manages the voter list?
(b) How is that officer's job different from that of the Returning Officer at the same district level?
