questions.a: (a) The Electoral Registration Officer (ERO). (b) The ERO manages the voter list, deciding who is on it and with what details; the Returning Officer (RO) conducts the election itself.
s: Part (a): Electoral Registration Officer
Part (b): ERO manages the voter list, RO conducts the election

questions.q: Justify the statement: 'The Model Code of Conduct helps keep elections free and fair.' Use its purpose, its three elements as the chapter gives them, and two kinds of complaint the ECI handles.
questions.a: Purpose: the code lists dos and don'ts for leaders, political parties and candidates to ensure free and fair elections. Element 1: the party in government must follow rules so that government resources are not used for the election; no new schemes or projects that may influence voters are announced. Element 2: all candidates must exercise discretion and restraint so that elections are peaceful. Element 3: influencing voters through gifts in return for votes is punishable. Complaints: gifts such as sarees and appliances to voters; abusive language against a rival; government officials campaigning for the ruling party; bundles of cash in a candidate's car. Each would tilt the contest by money, power or fear, which the code prevents.
s: Purpose of the code
Element on the party in government, with the example of new schemes
Elements on restraint and on gifts for votes
Two kinds of complaint described
Link: each would make the election unfair through money, power or fear

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Model Code of Conduct was first drawn up by T.N. Seshan after he became Chief Election Commissioner in 1990.
Reason (R): T.N. Seshan brought in strict vigilance on spending by candidates.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
(a) How many years passed between Shyam Saran Negi's first vote in the 1951 general elections and his vote in 2017?
(b) Link his vote at 100 to the chapter's closing point about the right to vote.
questions.a: (a) 2017 - 1951 = 66 years. (b) The chapter's closing points say that the right to vote is also a responsibility and has to be taken seriously by every voter; Negi's vote at 100 is an example of a voter still using the right after 66 years.
s: Part (a): 66 years
Part (b): the right to vote is also a responsibility, taken seriously

questions.q:
Read the statements about polling day.
1. The third polling officer inks the voter's finger and takes her signature.
2. The VVPAT replaces the EVM as the machine on which the vote is cast.
3. India's EVMs and VVPAT systems have been used in Namibia and Bhutan with support from the ECI.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 only
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Illustrative logs from two booths. At each booth the three polling officers of the chapter's process come first, and then the EVM; every voter who is allowed to vote passes the desks in order and then presses the button.
Booth A: first officer checked 900 voters; second officer inked 900 fingers; third officer took 900 chits; EVM recorded 900 button presses.
Booth B: first officer checked 900 voters; second officer inked 900 fingers; third officer took 896 chits; EVM recorded 896 button presses.
(a) How many voters at Booth B did not reach the EVM?
(b) At which desk's count does Booth B's log first differ from Booth A's?
(c) What percentage of the voters checked at Booth B pressed the button? Give one decimal place.
(d) The presiding officer of Booth B writes, 'The four were stopped at the third desk because their chits were wrong.' Does the log support this?
questions.a: (a) 900 - 896 = 4. (b) At the third officer's count of chits taken: 896 against 900. (c) 896 / 900 x 100 = 99.6 per cent. (d) No. The log shows only that four fewer chits were taken and four fewer presses were made; it does not say why. They may have left after the second desk for some other reason, so the officer's explanation is a guess that needs more evidence.
s: Part (a): 4 voters
Part (b): the third officer's chit count
Part (c): 99.6 per cent
Part (d): not supported; the log shows the gap, not its cause

questions.q:
Match each term in Column A with what it is, from the chapter, in Column B.
Column A: 1. EVM  2. VVPAT  3. NOTA  4. Reserved constituency
Column B: a. a printed paper record that lets the voter verify her vote and backs up a recount  b. the machine on which the voter presses a button and hears a beep  c. the option to reject all candidates  d. a constituency set aside for scheduled castes or scheduled tribes

Shyam Saran Negi, a school teacher in Himachal Pradesh, was the first voter in India's general elections of 1951, and he voted again in 2017 at the age of 100. About how old was he when he cast that first vote?
questions.a: About 34
o: About 34
About 66
About 18
About 51

questions.q:
Illustrative booth: 1,200 voters are registered, and 34 per cent of them stay away, as in the 2024 figure.
(a) How many voters come to the booth? (b) The chapter's process takes every voter past the first, second and third polling officers in turn. How many voters does each of the three polling officers deal with?
questions.a: (a) 34 per cent of 1,200 = 408 stay away, so 1,200 - 408 = 792 come. (b) Every voter passes all three desks, so each of the three polling officers deals with 792 voters.
s: Part (a): 792 voters come
Part (b): each officer deals with all 792, since every voter passes all three desks

questions.q: A first-time voter in Lucknow notes down the order of events at her polling station. Which order matches the chapter?
questions.a: Name and ID checked; finger inked and signature; chit and finger checked; button pressed
o: Name and ID checked; finger inked and signature; chit and finger checked; button pressed
Finger inked and signature; name and ID checked; chit and finger checked; button pressed
Name and ID checked; chit and finger checked; finger inked and signature; button pressed
Name and ID checked; finger inked and signature; button pressed; chit and finger checked

questions.q:
Describe the journey of a voter through a polling station in a Lok Sabha election, and analyse what each stage makes sure of.
(a) The first polling officer
(b) The second polling officer
(c) The third polling officer
(d) The EVM and the VVPAT (two marks)
questions.a: (a) Checks the voter's name on the voter list and her ID proof: only a registered voter, voting as herself, goes ahead. (b) Inks her finger, gives a chit and takes her signature: her visit is recorded and her finger is marked. (c) Takes the chit and checks the finger: only those who passed the earlier checks reach the machine; the NOTA option is also available. (d) She presses the button on the EVM and hears a beep, confirming the press; she checks the printed slip in the VVPAT, which lets her verify her vote and gives a paper backup for verification and recounting in case of disputes or failures.
s: Part (a): name and ID check; only the registered voter herself proceeds
Part (b): ink, chit and signature record the visit
Part (c): chit and finger checked before the machine; NOTA available
Part (d): EVM button and beep; VVPAT slip to verify and back up a recount

questions.q: Rahul has reached the third polling officer, who takes his chit and checks his finger. According to the chapter, which statement about what happens next is correct?
questions.a: He may choose NOTA instead of a candidate, then presses the EVM button
o: He may choose NOTA instead of a candidate, then presses the EVM button
He gets his finger inked now, before pressing the button on the EVM
He checks the printed VVPAT slip first and presses the button after that
He has his name and ID proof checked again before he can vote

questions.q:
(a) Which polling officer checks a voter's name on the voter list and her ID proof?
(b) The chapter says T.N. Seshan's voter IDs were meant to eliminate proxy voting. Explain how a voter ID helps the officer at that desk.
questions.a: (a) The first polling officer. (b) The voter ID gives the officer a document to check against the name on the voter list, so someone who is not the listed voter can be caught; this is how voter IDs help to end proxy voting.
s: Part (a): the first polling officer
Part (b): the ID is checked against the voter list, helping to end proxy voting

questions.q:
Of the 543 Lok Sabha constituencies, 84 are reserved for scheduled castes and 47 for scheduled tribes.
(a) How many constituencies are reserved in all, and how many are general?
(b) What percentage of the constituencies are general? Give one decimal place.
s: Part (a): 131 reserved, 412 general
Part (b): 75.9 per cent

questions.q:
Assertion (A): If the electronic count in a constituency is disputed, the votes can still be verified and recounted.
Reason (R): The VVPAT produces a physical paper record that serves as a backup for verification and recounting.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Illustrative: a Lok Sabha constituency has 1,200 polling stations. Each station is run by the three polling officers of the chapter's process, and no one else. At least how many polling officers of these three kinds does the constituency need in all?
Harish says: 'The VVPAT is useless, because the EVM already beeps when a vote is cast.' Test his claim and give your verdict with reasons.
questions.a: No. The beep only tells the voter that a button press was registered. The VVPAT gives a printed slip she can check, so she can verify that her vote was cast correctly; and the paper record is a backup for verification and recounting if there is a dispute or the electronic system fails. A beep cannot be recounted.
s: Verdict: no
The beep only confirms a press; the slip lets the voter verify her choice
The paper record backs up a recount in disputes or failures

questions.q: Taking the number of polling stations in 2024 as exactly 1 million, and the voters as 968 million, each polling station served about ___ voters on average.

A newspaper says, 'India has exported its elections to Namibia and Bhutan.' (a) What does the chapter say was used there, and with whose support? (b) Say why the chapter's wording is narrower than the newspaper's.
questions.a: (a) India's electronic voting machines (EVMs) and VVPAT systems have been used in Namibia and Bhutan with support from the Election Commission of India. (b) The chapter speaks only of the technology being used, with ECI support (and other countries studying it and receiving training from India); it does not say that India runs or conducts elections there.
s: Part (a): EVMs and VVPAT used there, with ECI support
Part (b): the chapter speaks of technology and training, not of India conducting the elections

questions.q: True or False? 'The VVPAT slip is a second vote that gets added to the EVM's count.' Give the verdict and the correct statement.
questions.a: False. The VVPAT produces a physical paper record that lets the voter verify that her electronic vote was cast correctly; it is a backup used for verification and recounting in case of disputes or failures of the electronic system, not an extra vote.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: it is a paper record to verify the vote and a backup for recounting

questions.q:
Illustrative results. Constituency 1: Candidate P 4,12,350 votes, Candidate Q 4,11,980. Constituency 2: Candidate R 6,05,000, Candidate S 5,64,000. In each, the losing candidate complains that the EVMs at three polling stations stopped working properly, and 1,150 votes were cast at those three stations in each constituency.
(a) What was the winning margin in each constituency?
(b) What physical record exists that can be used to check the votes at those stations?
(c) According to the chapter, in which two kinds of situation is that record meant to be used?
(d) In which constituency are the votes at those three stations enough, in number, to have changed the winner? What can still be done with the record in the other?
questions.a: (a) 4,12,350 - 4,11,980 = 370 votes in Constituency 1; 6,05,000 - 5,64,000 = 41,000 in Constituency 2. (b) The VVPAT slips: the paper record printed when each vote was cast. (c) In case of disputes or of failures of the electronic system, for verification and recounting. (d) Constituency 1: 1,150 votes at the three stations is more than the margin of 370. In Constituency 2 they are fewer than 41,000, so they cannot change the winner; the slips are still a backup for verification and recounting in a dispute.
s: Part (a): 370 and 41,000
Part (b): the VVPAT slips
Part (c): disputes and failures of the electronic system
Part (d): Constituency 1 (1,150 > 370); in Constituency 2 the slips remain a backup for verification

questions.q:
Use the chapter's figures for the 2024 Lok Sabha election: about 968 million voters, 543 constituencies, over 1 million polling stations, 84 constituencies reserved for scheduled castes and 47 for scheduled tribes.
(a) About how many voters did one constituency have on average? Give the answer in millions to two decimal places.
(b) On average, each constituency had more than how many polling stations? Round down to a whole number.
(c) What percentage of constituencies was reserved? Give one decimal place.
(d) Using (a) and (b), explain why the chapter says many people, including teachers, are deployed for elections.
questions.a: (a) 968 / 543 = about 1.78 million voters. (b) 1,000,000 / 543 = 1,841.6, so more than 1,841 polling stations per constituency on average. (c) 131 / 543 x 100 = 24.1 per cent. (d) Each constituency must serve close to 1.8 million voters at well over 1,800 polling stations, every one of which needs a team of polling officers (three per booth in the process described), so far more staff are needed than the ECI's own officers; many people, including teachers, are deployed.
s: Part (a): about 1.78 million
Part (b): more than 1,841 polling stations
Part (c): 24.1 per cent
Part (d): the numbers need many polling teams, so teachers and others are deployed

questions.q: Pooja claims: 'Roughly one out of every four Lok Sabha constituencies is reserved for scheduled castes or scheduled tribes.' Test her claim with the chapter's figures and give your verdict.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. 84 constituencies are reserved for scheduled castes and 47 for scheduled tribes, 131 in all. 131 / 543 = about 24.1 per cent, which is close to one in four (25 per cent); the other 412 are general.
s: Verdict: yes
131 reserved out of 543
131 / 543 is about 24 per cent, close to one in four

questions.q: Show that, by the process the chapter describes, a person cannot reach the EVM without being identified and recorded. Use the work of each of the three polling officers.
questions.a: The first polling officer checks her name on the voter list and her ID proof, so she must be a listed voter. The second inks her finger, gives her a chit and takes her signature, so her finger is marked and her signature taken. The third takes the chit and checks the finger, so only someone who passed the first two stages moves on. Only then does she press the button on the EVM.
s: First officer: name on the list and ID proof
Second officer: ink, chit and signature
Third officer: chit taken and finger checked before the EVM

questions.q: Differentiate between an MP elected to the Lok Sabha and an MLA, by where each sits and the kind of issues each mainly focuses on.
questions.a: An MP elected to the Lok Sabha represents a constituency in the national Parliament and focuses on issues affecting the entire country. An MLA represents a constituency in the state (or union territory) legislative assembly and focuses primarily on regional issues. Both are chosen through similar electoral processes but work at different levels of governance.
s: MP: national Parliament, issues of the whole country
MLA: state assembly, mainly regional issues

questions.q:
Trace how the votes cast in a general election turn into a national government.
(a) How is the country divided for the Lok Sabha election, and what are the winners called?
(b) How is the winner in each constituency decided? Use the chapter's example.
(c) How is the government formed from the results?
(d) What happens if no single party wins enough seats, and who becomes prime minister?
questions.a: (a) Into 543 constituencies; each elects one Member of Parliament (MP). (b) By First-Past-the-Post: the candidate with the most votes wins, even without 50 per cent, as Gurmat won with 12 votes against Ravi's 10 and Ahmed's 8. (c) The party or coalition winning a majority of the seats in the Lok Sabha forms the national government. (d) Two or more parties can work together as a coalition to reach a majority; the leader of the majority typically becomes the prime minister.
s: Part (a): 543 constituencies, each electing an MP
Part (b): First-Past-the-Post with the Gurmat example
Part (c): majority of seats forms the government
Part (d): coalition to reach a majority; its leader usually becomes prime minister

questions.q: Leela, who lives in a village in Telangana, has three concerns: the national policy on railway fares, a broken state highway near her village, and the national policy on fertiliser supply. For each, say whether she should mainly approach her MP or her MLA, and give the reason from the chapter.
questions.a: Railway fares: her MP, because Lok Sabha members focus on issues affecting the entire country. State highway: her MLA, because members of the state legislative assembly focus primarily on regional issues. Fertiliser supply policy for the country: her MP, again a national issue.
s: Railway fares to the MP, a national issue
State highway to the MLA, a regional issue
National fertiliser policy to the MP, with the reason

questions.q: True or False? 'In every state of India the legislative assembly is called the Vidhan Sabha.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the legislative assembly is called by several names in regional languages, for example Vidhan Sabha and Niyama Sabha; whatever it is called, its members are the MLAs.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: regional languages use several names, such as Vidhan Sabha and Niyama Sabha

questions.q: Two different 'majorities' matter after a general election. (a) What must a candidate have to win a constituency, and what must a party or coalition have to form the national government? (b) Explain why a candidate can win a seat without a majority of the votes in her constituency.
questions.a: (a) To win a constituency a candidate needs the most votes of any candidate; to form the national government a party or coalition needs a majority of the seats in the Lok Sabha. (b) Under First-Past-the-Post the candidate with the most votes wins, even without 50 per cent of the votes, as Gurmat won her class election with more votes than Ravi or Ahmed but not more than half.
s: Part (a): most votes for a seat; a majority of seats for the government
Part (b): First-Past-the-Post needs the most votes, not half

questions.q: In the Suryodaya class election, Gurmat got 12 votes, Ravi 10 and Ahmed 8, and one ballot was invalid. Which statement about her win is correct?
questions.a: She had the most votes, though not a majority of the ballots
o: She had the most votes, though not a majority of the ballots
She won because 12 is more than half of the ballots cast
She should not have won, as no candidate had half the ballots
She won only after Ravi's votes were added to her own

questions.q: After a general election a coalition of three parties forms the national government. Which description of its position fits the chapter?
questions.a: Its parties together hold a majority of the seats in the Lok Sabha
o: Its parties together hold a majority of the seats in the Lok Sabha
The Chief Election Commissioner chose it after the results were counted
Each of its parties won every seat in the constituencies it contested
Its parties together hold a majority of the seats in the Rajya Sabha

questions.q: Sameer says: 'Local body elections in my town follow the same basic rule of universal adult franchise as Lok Sabha elections, even though a different commission conducts them.' Test his claim and give your verdict with reasons.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. Elections to local bodies are conducted by the State Election Commission, not by the ECI directly, though it works in consultation with the ECI. The chapter says universal adult franchise, and all other constitutional provisions that apply to direct elections by the people, apply to these local elections too; Article 326 also lists all local elections in villages and cities.
s: Verdict: yes
A different body: the State Election Commission, consulting the ECI
Universal adult franchise and the same constitutional provisions apply to local elections

questions.q:
Illustrative result in one Lok Sabha constituency: Candidate A 3,10,000 votes; Candidate B 2,90,000; Candidate C 1,50,000; Candidate D 50,000; NOTA 10,000. A newspaper headline reads: 'A wins with a majority of the votes'.
(a) How many votes were recorded in all, counting NOTA?
(b) What percentage of these did A get? Give one decimal place.
(c) Correct the headline.
(d) B's supporters demand that a winner must have more than half of all the votes recorded. How many votes would that need here, does any candidate meet it, and which rule does India use instead?
questions.a: (a) 3,10,000 + 2,90,000 + 1,50,000 + 50,000 + 10,000 = 8,10,000. (b) 3,10,000 / 8,10,000 x 100 = 38.3 per cent. (c) 'A wins with the most votes' (38.3 per cent, not a majority). (d) Half of 8,10,000 is 4,05,000, so more than that is needed, and no candidate has it (A has 3,10,000). India uses First-Past-the-Post, under which the candidate with the most votes, here A, wins even without 50 per cent.
s: Part (b): 38.3 per cent
Part (c): A won with the most votes, not a majority
Part (d): more than 4,05,000 needed and nobody has it; India uses First-Past-the-Post, so A wins

questions.q:
Illustrative result of a ward election to a city's municipal corporation: Priya 1,800 votes, Qadir 1,650, Rohit 1,200, NOTA 150; 50 ballots were invalid. Qadir and Rohit had made very similar promises about drains and streetlights.
(a) Who wins, and what share of the 4,800 valid votes (candidates plus NOTA) did the winner get?
(b) Which body conducts this election, and with whom does it consult?
(c) Rohit says he will not contest next time. Suppose all other voters vote as before and Rohit's 1,200 voters split two to one in favour of Qadir over Priya. Predict the new result.
(d) What does your answer to (c) show about how First-Past-the-Post can work when similar candidates split the vote?
questions.a: (a) Priya, with the most votes; 1,800 / 4,800 = 37.5 per cent. (b) The State Election Commission, in consultation with the Election Commission of India. (c) Qadir gets 800 more (1,650 + 800 = 2,450) and Priya 400 more (1,800 + 400 = 2,200), so Qadir would win. (d) Under First-Past-the-Post only the most votes count, so when two candidates with similar promises split their voters, a third candidate can win even though more voters preferred what the other two offered.
s: Part (a): Priya, 37.5 per cent
Part (b): State Election Commission, consulting the ECI
Part (c): Qadir 2,450 against Priya 2,200, so Qadir wins
Part (d): split votes can let a third candidate win under First-Past-the-Post

questions.q: A 100-seat state assembly returns P 44 seats, Q 30 and R 26. Following the chapter's rule on forming a government, which of these arrangements can NOT form it?
questions.a: P alone
o: P alone
P and R together
Q and R together
P and Q together

questions.q:
Illustrative seat count after a general election to a house of 543 seats, with four parties: Party A 230 seats, Party B 190, Party C 70, Party D 53. After the results, Parties A and D announce that they will work together, and Parties B and C announce the same.
(a) What is the smallest number of seats that makes a majority in this house?
(b) Can Party A, the largest party, form the national government alone? Explain.
(c) How many seats does each of the two groups hold?
(d) Predict which group forms the national government, and who usually becomes prime minister.
questions.a: (a) More than half of 543: 272 seats. (b) No: 230 is fewer than 272, so A alone does not have a majority. (c) A and D: 230 + 53 = 283; B and C: 190 + 70 = 260. (d) The A-D coalition, with 283 seats (a majority), forms the national government; the leader of this majority typically becomes the prime minister. B-C, with 260, falls short.
s: Part (a): 272 seats
Part (b): no, 230 is short of 272
Part (c): 283 and 260
Part (d): the A-D coalition governs; its leader usually becomes prime minister

questions.a: (a) Lok Sabha: national level, issues affecting the entire country. Assembly: state or union territory level, mainly regional issues. (b) Members of Parliament (MPs) and Members of Legislative Assembly (MLAs); the assembly is called Vidhan Sabha or Niyama Sabha in some regional languages. (c) The same in both: First-Past-the-Post, the candidate with the most votes wins. (d) In the Lok Sabha, the party or coalition with a majority of seats forms the national government and its leader typically becomes prime minister; in the assembly, the party or coalition with a majority forms the state government and its leader becomes chief minister.
s: Part (a): national against state level and issues
Part (b): MPs and MLAs; Vidhan Sabha or Niyama Sabha
Part (c): First-Past-the-Post in both
Part (d): prime minister and chief minister from the majority in each house

questions.q:
Read the statements about direct elections.
1. Under First-Past-the-Post, a candidate can win a constituency without getting even half of the votes.
2. In some regional languages the state legislative assembly is called Vidhan Sabha or Niyama Sabha.
3. The leader of the largest party in the Lok Sabha always becomes prime minister, even if the party does not have a majority.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: In a constituency 1,000 valid votes are shared among five candidates. Under First-Past-the-Post, the smallest number of votes with which one candidate can still win outright is ___.

The chapter notes that a Lok Sabha constituency may have two or more assembly constituencies. Suppose a Lok Sabha constituency contains exactly 7 assembly constituencies, each lying wholly inside it and electing one MLA.
(a) How many MPs and how many MLAs do its voters elect directly in all?
(b) How many of each does a single voter in it help elect?
questions.a: (a) 1 MP for the whole Lok Sabha constituency and 7 MLAs, one for each assembly constituency. (b) One MP and one MLA: she votes in her own assembly constituency for one MLA and in the larger Lok Sabha constituency for one MP.
s: Part (a): 1 MP and 7 MLAs
Part (b): one MP and one MLA for each voter

questions.q: A municipal corporation election is due in Pune. Which statement about it is correct by the chapter?
questions.a: Universal adult franchise applies here as in a general election

The ECI's Returning Officer for the Lok Sabha seat conducts it
The councillors elected are called Members of Parliament

questions.a: It is the state legislative assembly; its members are MLAs
o: It is the state legislative assembly; its members are MLAs
It is the Rajya Sabha, whose members are chosen by MLAs
It is the Lok Sabha under its name in a regional language
It is the State Election Commission, by another name

questions.q: Nikhil says: 'In India the voters directly elect the prime minister, just as they elect their MP.' Test his claim and give your verdict with reasons.
questions.a: No. Voters directly elect only the MP of their own Lok Sabha constituency. After the results, the party or coalition that wins a majority of the seats in the Lok Sabha forms the national government, and the leader of this majority typically becomes prime minister. So the prime minister comes from the majority of elected MPs, not from a separate vote by all the people.
s: Verdict: no
Voters elect only their constituency's MP
The leader of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha usually becomes prime minister

questions.q:
A 100-seat state assembly returns M 38 seats, N 30, O 22 and P 10. N, O and P agree to work together.
(a) Can M, the largest party, form the government? (b) Who forms it, and who becomes the chief minister, as the chapter describes it?
questions.a: (a) No: a majority of 100 seats needs 51, and M has only 38. (b) N, O and P together hold 30 + 22 + 10 = 62 seats, a majority, so this coalition forms the government, and its leader typically becomes the chief minister.
s: Part (a): no, 38 is short of the 51 needed
Part (b): the N-O-P coalition (62 seats) forms it; its leader typically becomes chief minister

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Candidates elected to the Lok Sabha are known as Members of Parliament.
Reason (R): India uses the First-Past-the-Post system, in which the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Riya says: 'Every Member of Parliament gets a vote in the election of the President.' Test her claim and give your verdict with reasons.
questions.a: No. The electoral college includes the MPs of both Houses, but the 12 nominated members of the Rajya Sabha are left out. Only elected MPs vote (along with the elected MLAs of the states, Delhi and Puducherry), so that only directly elected representatives choose the President. (Nominated MPs do vote for the Vice President.)
s: Verdict: no
The 12 nominated Rajya Sabha members are excluded
Reason: only directly elected representatives vote

questions.q: Differentiate between a direct and an indirect election, giving one school example and one national example of each from the chapter.
questions.a: Direct: the people themselves vote for their representative; for example, the Suryodaya students electing their class representative, or voters electing their Lok Sabha MP or MLA. Indirect: representatives who were themselves elected choose the next set; for example, class representatives electing a school council, or MLAs electing members of the Rajya Sabha (or the electoral college electing the President).
s: Direct: people vote themselves, with a school and a national example
Indirect: elected representatives choose, with a school and a national example

questions.q:
Read the statements about indirect elections.
1. The Rajya Sabha is never dissolved, and one-third of its members retire every two years.
2. Every state gets the same number of Rajya Sabha seats, whatever its population.
3. The Vice President is the chairperson of the Rajya Sabha.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Compare the elections of the President and the Vice President of India.
(a) Who forms each electoral college?
(b) Name two groups that vote for one but not the other, and say which.
(c) What voting system is used in each?
(d) What does each office have to do with the Rajya Sabha or with the other office?
questions.a: (a) President: elected MPs of both Houses and elected MLAs of the states and of Delhi and Puducherry. Vice President: elected and nominated members of both Houses of Parliament. (b) Nominated members of the Rajya Sabha vote for the Vice President but not the President; MLAs vote for the President but not the Vice President. (c) The single transferable vote system in both. (d) The Vice President is chairperson of the Rajya Sabha and steps in when the President cannot discharge the functions of the office; the President nominates 12 members of the Rajya Sabha.
s: Part (a): the two electoral colleges
Part (b): nominated RS members (VP only) and MLAs (President only)
Part (c): single transferable vote in both
Part (d): VP chairs the Rajya Sabha and stands in for the President

questions.q:
The Rajya Sabha has 245 members, of whom the President nominates 12.
(a) What percentage of its members are nominated? Give one decimal place.
(b) Who elects the rest, and why does this make the Rajya Sabha election indirect?
questions.a: (a) 12 / 245 x 100 = 4.9 per cent. (b) The other 233 are elected by the elected members of the state legislative assemblies (MLAs). It is indirect because the voters are representatives who were themselves elected by the people, not the people themselves.
s: Part (a): 4.9 per cent
Part (b): 233 elected by MLAs, who were themselves elected, so it is indirect

questions.q: The chapter names three challenges facing India's electoral system. For each one, explain how it harms a free and fair election, and link it to one step from the chapter's 'road ahead' or from an earlier reform in the chapter.
questions.a: Growing influence of money: votes can be bought or the contest tilted to the richest; links to vigilance on candidates' spending (Seshan) or the code's ban on gifts for votes. Candidates with criminal records: voters may be pushed to choose among unfit candidates; links to empowering voters with information to make thoughtful choices. Voter apathy, especially in urban areas: many people do not use their vote, so results reflect fewer voices; links to media, education and awareness campaigns, especially for the youth.
s: Money: harm and a matching remedy
Criminal records: harm and a matching remedy
Voter apathy: harm and a matching remedy

questions.q: In an illustrative ward of a big city, only 4 of every 10 registered voters cast a vote, though polling stations are close by and the voters face no barrier. Which challenge named at the end of the chapter does this show?
questions.a: Voter apathy, especially in urban areas
o: Voter apathy, especially in urban areas
The growing influence of money in polls
Candidates with criminal records
Gifts offered in return for votes

questions.q:
Illustrative case: a state has 12 seats in the Rajya Sabha, with one-third of them falling vacant every two years. In 2027 a new party wins a large majority in the state's legislative assembly.
(a) How many of the state's Rajya Sabha seats fall vacant at each two-yearly election?
(b) Who votes to fill them?
(c) A member from this state elected in 2026 serves a full term. In which year does she retire, and how many two-yearly elections for the state's seats fall between her election year and her retirement year (not counting either)?
(d) Predict whether all 12 of the state's Rajya Sabha members can be replaced at the 2028 election, and say how many two-yearly elections are needed at the least before every one of the 12 seats can have changed hands.
questions.a: (a) One-third of 12 = 4 seats. (b) The elected members of the state legislative assembly (MLAs). (c) She retires in 2032, after a six-year term; the two-yearly elections in between fall in 2028 and 2030, so two. (d) No. Only 4 seats fall vacant in 2028; the other 8 members keep their six-year terms, because the Rajya Sabha is never dissolved and one-third retire every two years. At least three two-yearly elections (for example 2028, 2030 and 2032) are needed before all 12 seats can change hands.
s: Part (a): 4 seats
Part (b): the state's elected MLAs
Part (c): retires in 2032; two elections in between (2028, 2030)
Part (d): no; only 4 seats in 2028, so at least three biennial elections are needed

questions.q: The Vice President is elected by the elected and nominated members of both Houses of Parliament. Taking the Lok Sabha as 543 members and the Rajya Sabha as 245, this electoral college has ___ members.
In a school in Bhubaneswar, the twelve class representatives, each elected by their own class, meet to choose the head of the school council. Which Indian election works in the same way?
questions.a: MLAs electing members of the Rajya Sabha
o: MLAs electing members of the Rajya Sabha
Voters of a constituency electing an MP
Voters of a constituency electing an MLA
Villagers electing their gram panchayat

questions.q:
Justify the chapter's statement: 'An aware and vigilant voter is the strongest safeguard of a democratic system.'
(a) Explain the three challenges the chapter names.
(b) Show how an aware voter can weaken each one.
(c) Name two means the chapter says must work together to build such voters.
questions.a: (a) The growing influence of money in elections; a significant proportion of candidates with criminal records; voter apathy, particularly in urban areas. (b) An aware voter refuses gifts or cash in return for votes and reports them; she finds out about candidates' records and does not vote for those she judges unfit; she treats voting as a responsibility and votes rather than staying home. (c) Any two of media, education and awareness campaigns, which must work together to help people, especially the youth, understand the importance of voting wisely.
s: Part (a): the three challenges
Part (b): how an aware voter counters each
Part (c): two of media, education and awareness campaigns

questions.a: An elected MLA of the Puducherry assembly
o: An elected MLA of the Puducherry assembly
A nominated member of the Delhi assembly
An elected member of a state's Legislative Council
A nominated member of the Rajya Sabha

questions.a: So that only directly elected representatives choose the President
o: So that only directly elected representatives choose the President
So that nominated members cannot vote in the Vice President's election either
So that the Lok Sabha alone, and not the Rajya Sabha, chooses the President
So that smaller states get fair representation, as with the single transferable vote

questions.q:
(a) Why does Uttar Pradesh have more Rajya Sabha seats than Arunachal Pradesh?
(b) A student says: 'The single transferable vote gives every state the same number of seats.' Use the chapter to correct her.
questions.a: (a) Seats are allotted to each state based on population, and Uttar Pradesh is more populous than Arunachal Pradesh. (b) The chapter says seats follow population, so states do not get equal numbers; the single transferable vote is a special way of voting meant to ensure that smaller states also get fair representation.
s: Part (a): seats follow population
Part (b): STV is about fair representation of smaller states, not equal seats; seats follow population

Match each office or seat in Column A with the people in Column B who elect it.
Column A: 1. The 233 elected members of the Rajya Sabha  2. The President  3. The Vice President  4. A Lok Sabha MP

Dr. Menon is one of the 12 members of the Rajya Sabha nominated by the President. In which of these elections can she vote?

o: The Vice President's election only
The President's election only
Both the President's and the Vice President's
Neither of the two elections

questions.q: True or False? 'Because the Rajya Sabha is called the Permanent House, its members stay in office for life.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. 'Permanent' means the Rajya Sabha is never dissolved as a house. Each member has a six-year term, and one-third of the members retire every two years, when new members are elected.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the house is never dissolved, but members serve six-year terms with one-third retiring every two years

questions.q: Show that all the members of the Rajya Sabha can never be replaced by newly elected members at one single election.
questions.a: The Rajya Sabha is the Permanent House and is never dissolved, so there is no moment when the whole house ends and a fresh one is elected. Each member has a six-year term, and one-third of the members retire every two years; at each election only those seats are filled, while the other two-thirds continue. So at any election at least two-thirds of the members stay on.
s: Never dissolved, so no general replacement
Six-year terms with one-third retiring every two years
So each election fills only about one-third; two-thirds continue

questions.q:
A student writes: 'Over 968 million people could vote in 2024, yet the President, who represents the whole country, is chosen only by members of Parliament and of the state assemblies, a small group beside 968 million voters. This is an odd result for a democracy.' The chapter's figures: the Lok Sabha has 543 elected members and the Rajya Sabha 233 elected and 12 nominated members.
(a) How many members of Parliament are in the President's electoral college?
(b) Which members of the Rajya Sabha are left out, and why?
(c) Who else is in the electoral college, and what does the chapter say this mix ensures?
(d) Suppose the 12 nominated members of the Rajya Sabha were also allowed to vote. By what percentage would the Parliament part of the college grow, to one decimal place, and which of the chapter's reasons for excluding them would then be broken?
questions.a: (a) 543 + 233 = 776 elected MPs. (b) The 12 nominated members, because only directly elected representatives vote. (c) The elected MLAs of the states and of Delhi and Puducherry; since the President represents the whole country, this ensures the support of both the central and state governments. (d) 12 / 776 x 100 = 1.5 per cent. The reason broken would be that only directly elected representatives choose the President: the 12 are nominated by the President, not elected by the people.
s: Part (a): 776 elected MPs
Part (b): 12 nominated members excluded; only directly elected representatives vote
Part (c): elected MLAs of states, Delhi and Puducherry; support of centre and states
Part (d): 1.5 per cent; only directly elected representatives would no longer choose

questions.q:

(b) What role does this person hold in Parliament at other times?

s: Part (a): the Vice President
Part (b): chairperson of the Rajya Sabha
